fiji: Fiji is an archipelago of 332 islands, of which 106 are inhabited, and 522 smaller islets, in the South Pacific about 2,000 km north-northeast of New Zealand. Only around 10% of its area of some 194,000 square kilometres is land. The two largest islands, Viti Levu and Vanua Levu, account for about three-quarters of the land area. The islands are mountainous, with peaks up to 1,324 metres, and covered with thick tropical forest. Most were formed by volcanic activity beginning around 150 million years ago. The 180° meridian runs through Taveuni, but the International Date Line is bent so that the whole group keeps one time.

Pottery shows that Austronesian peoples had settled Fiji by at least 3500 to 1000 BCE, with Melanesians following about a thousand years later. It is believed that either the Lapita people or the ancestors of the Polynesians settled first, though not much is known of what became of them. Archaeological evidence shows settlement on Moturiki Island from at least 600 BCE and possibly 900 BCE, and some migrants moved on to Samoa, Tonga and even Hawai'i. Trade with neighbouring archipelagos began long before European contact. In the 10th century the Tu'i Tonga Empire was established in Tonga and Fiji came within its sphere of influence, bringing Polynesian customs and language; that empire began to decline in the 13th century.

Europeans first visited in the 17th century. The name Fiji comes from the Tongan pronunciation, Fisi, of the Fijian name Viti, and was first promulgated by Captain James Cook; accounts written until the late 19th century spelled it Feejee. After a brief period as an independent kingdom, the British established the Colony of Fiji in 1874. It was a Crown colony until it gained independence in 1970 as the Dominion of Fiji. After a series of coups, the military government declared a republic in 1987.

Fiji is a parliamentary republic with its capital at Suva on Viti Levu, home to nearly three-quarters of the population. About 54.3% of the people are native Fijians, who are Melanesians with Polynesian ancestry in many cases, and 38.1% are Indo-Fijians, descendants of Indian contract labourers brought by the British in the 19th century. Rotuma, with a culture closer to Tonga and Samoa, has a special administrative status. Rugby sevens is the national sport.
finland: Finland lies approximately between latitudes 60° and 70° N, and only Reykjavík lies further north among world capitals than Helsinki. Its land is predominantly covered by boreal forest, and it has about 168,000 lakes and 179,000 islands; the largest lake, Saimaa, is the fourth largest in Europe. Much of the landscape is a result of the Ice Age, and the terrain is rising by about 1 centimetre a year around the Gulf of Bothnia because of post-glacial rebound, so that the surface area of the country expands by about 7 square kilometres annually. Halti, at 1,324 metres, is the highest point.

The area was settled around 8500 BCE towards the end of the last glacial period, by hunter-gatherers using stone tools. The first pottery appeared in 5200 BCE with the Comb Ceramic culture, and the Corded Ware culture arrived in the south of coastal Finland between 3000 and 2500 BCE and may have coincided with the start of agriculture. In the Iron Age, Finland Proper was the most densely populated area, and main exports were furs, slaves, castoreum and falcons to European courts. At the end of the ninth century, local artefacts had more common features than ever before, which has been interpreted as expressing a common Finnish identity.

From the middle of the 13th century Finland became part of Sweden during the Northern Crusades. In 1809, as a result of the Finnish War, it was captured from Sweden and became an autonomous grand duchy within the Russian Empire, and an independence movement gradually developed. Finland declared its independence after the Russian Revolution of 1917, and a civil war the following year ended in victory for the anticommunist Whites. During World War II Finland fought the Soviet Union in the Winter War and the Continuation War and Nazi Germany in the Lapland War, losing parts of its territory but retaining its independence and democracy.

Finland has a population of 5.7 million, and Helsinki is the capital and largest city. The official languages are Finnish and Swedish, the mother tongues of 83.5 percent and 5.0 percent of the population. It became the first country in Europe to grant universal suffrage in 1906. A new constitution enacted in 2000 made the presidency primarily a ceremonial office, and Finland is now considered a parliamentary republic. It joined the European Union in 1995 and the Eurozone in 1999, and NATO in 2023. National minorities include the Sámi, Roma, Jews and Tatars.
finnish-war: After concluding the Treaty of Tilsit with Napoleon in 1807, Emperor Alexander I of Russia wrote on 24 September 1807 to King Gustav IV Adolf of Sweden that peace between them depended on Sweden accepting the treaty's limits, which in practice meant cutting off trade with Britain. The king, who viewed Napoleon as the Antichrist, secured an alliance with Britain on 8 February 1808. In Saint Petersburg his stubbornness was seen as a convenient pretext for occupying Finland. Swedish plans assumed that war in winter was impossible, while Russian planners chose a winter offensive, when frozen seas would isolate Finland.

On 21 February 1808, 24,000 Russian troops under Friedrich Wilhelm von Buxhoeveden crossed the border and took Loviisa; war was not declared until April. Helsinki fell on 2 March and Turku on 21 March, as the Swedish army under General Wilhelm Mauritz Klingspor withdrew northwards. Sveaborg, with a garrison of 6,000 men and over 700 cannons, surrendered on 6 May 1808 after prolonged negotiations, its commander Admiral Carl Olof Cronstedt believing resistance futile, and the Russians gained most of the Swedish archipelago fleet intact. Swedish counter-attacks at Siikajoki and Revolax halted the offensive for a time, and Finns rose in guerrilla fighting.

Reinforced to 55,000 men against an estimated 36,000, the Russians attacked again in August, and Count Nikolay Kamensky won the most important victory at Oravais on 14 September. By November 1808 Russian forces had overrun all of Finland, and the Convention of Olkijoki of 19 November obliged the Swedish army to leave. In March 1809 Russian columns crossed the frozen Gulf of Bothnia, occupying the Åland Islands and entering Umeå on 24 March. King Gustav IV, blamed for the loss of Finland, was dethroned by a coup in Stockholm on 13 March, and his uncle became Charles XIII of Sweden.

By the Treaty of Fredrikshamn of 17 September 1809 Sweden also gave up its domains east of the Torne river. The Grand Duchy of Finland kept the Gustavian constitution of 1772 with only slight modifications until 1919, and in 1812 Russia attached to it the areas it had gained from Sweden in the 18th century, known as Old Finland. In Sweden the war was followed by a new constitution and, in 1818, by the establishment of the House of Bernadotte. Two studies of 2015 by the political scientists Jan Teorell and Bo Rothstein argue that the defeat moved Swedish elites to reform the bureaucracy.
first-world-war: For much of the 19th century the major European powers kept a tenuous balance known as the Concert of Europe. Victory in the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–1871 allowed Otto von Bismarck to consolidate a German Empire, and French policy then aimed to avenge the defeat. Germany and Austria-Hungary formed the Dual Alliance in 1879, which became the Triple Alliance when Italy joined in 1882.

On 28 June 1914 Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir presumptive to Emperor Franz Joseph I, visited Sarajevo. Six assassins of the Young Bosnia movement lined his route. A grenade injured two aides, but an hour later Gavrilo Princip shot and fatally wounded the Archduke and his wife Sophie.

Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July, and Russia mobilised in Serbia's defence. In early August Germany declared war on Russia and France, and the United Kingdom entered after Germany invaded Belgium. The German advance was halted in September, and the Western Front settled into a near-continuous line of trenches. Battles at Verdun, the Somme and Passchendaele failed to break the stalemate.

The Ottoman Empire joined the Central Powers in November 1914. The United States joined the Allies in April 1917 after Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare, and Soviet Russia made a separate peace in March 1918. The Allied Hundred Days Offensive from August 1918 collapsed the German front line, and the war ended with the Armistice of 11 November 1918.

Four dynasties fell: the Romanovs, the Hohenzollerns, the Habsburgs and the Ottomans. Poland, Finland, the Baltic states, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia were among the new states. Under the Treaty of Versailles, signed on 28 June 1919, Germany lost territory, was disarmed and had to pay large reparations.

Estimates put the deaths at 15 to 22 million and about 23 million wounded military personnel. Of 60 million European military personnel mobilised, an estimated 8 million were killed. The war also drew women into industry in unprecedented numbers, which aided the struggle for women's voting rights.
florida: About two-thirds of Florida occupies a peninsula between the Gulf of Mexico, the Atlantic Ocean and the Straits of Florida, and it extends northwest into a panhandle. It is the only state that borders both the Gulf and the Atlantic, and it has the longest coastline in the contiguous United States, about 2,170 kilometres. Its climate varies from subtropical in the north to tropical in the south. Everglades National Park is the largest tropical wilderness in the United States, and the Florida Reef is the only living coral barrier reef in the continental United States.

The first inhabitants, the Paleo-Indians, entered Florida at least 14,000 years ago. By the 16th century the major groups included the Apalachee, the Timucua, the Ais, the Mayaimi, the Tequesta and the Calusa. Juan Ponce de León sighted the peninsula on 2 April 1513, and it was the first region of what is now the contiguous United States to be visited and settled by Europeans. The story that he sought the Fountain of Youth is apocryphal and appeared only long after his death. An estimated 700,000 Native Americans lived in Florida in the 1520s, but by 1700 only around 2,000 remained.

Spain founded St. Augustine in 1565, the oldest continuously inhabited European-established settlement in the United States. Britain held Florida briefly from 1763, and Spain recovered it in 1783. Spain ceded it to the United States in 1821. It was the main location of the Seminole Wars (1816–1858), became the 27th state on 3 March 1845, and seceded on 10 January 1861 as one of the seven original Confederate States, returning to the Union on 25 June 1868.

Florida is a state of the United States, with Tallahassee as its capital and 67 counties. Its most populous city is Jacksonville, and the Miami metropolitan area is the largest in the state. Miami Beach's Art Deco District belongs to the state's large collection of Art Deco and Streamline Moderne buildings, and St. Augustine preserves Spanish revival and other early styles.
france: Celtic tribes known as Gauls settled the area in the Iron Age. Ionian Greeks from Phocaea founded Massalia around 600 BCE, and the Romans conquered the south of Gaul around 125 BCE. Julius Caesar conquered the rest and overcame a revolt by the Gallic chieftain Vercingetorix in 52 BCE, after which Gaul was divided into provinces and a Gallo-Roman culture developed. In the 5th century the Visigoths, the Burgundians and the Franks settled in the region. The Franks formed the kingdom of Francia, the heartland of the Carolingian Empire, and the Treaty of Verdun of 843 partitioned that empire, with West Francia evolving into the Kingdom of France.

In the High Middle Ages France was a powerful but decentralised feudal kingdom. After Philip II defeated the Angevin Empire and won the Battle of Bouvines, it became more centralised. From the mid-14th to the mid-15th centuries a dynastic conflict with England, the Hundred Years' War, followed. The 16th century brought the French Renaissance, the French Wars of Religion between Catholics and Huguenots, and the emergence of a French colonial empire. Under Louis XIV the nation built Europe's strongest army.

The French Revolution of 1789 overthrew the ancien régime and produced the Declaration of the Rights of Man. Napoleon Bonaparte established the First French Empire and subjugated much of continental Europe. Later came the Bourbon Restoration, the Second Republic and the Second French Empire under Napoleon III, which collapsed during the Franco-Prussian War in 1870 and gave way to the Third Republic. France emerged victorious from World War I at great human and economic cost, and surrendered and was occupied by Germany in 1940. After liberation in 1944 the Fourth Republic was established and later dissolved over the course of the Algerian War. Charles de Gaulle formed the Fifth Republic in 1958, and Algeria and most French colonies became independent in the 1960s.

Metropolitan France covers 551,500 square kilometres and is bordered by the Pyrenees, the Alps, the Jura Mountains and the Rhine along much of its edge. The estimated population is 69,081,996, and Paris is the capital. France is a unitary semi-presidential republic under the Constitution of 1958, with a president elected for five years and a bicameral Parliament. It is one of the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council and has 54 UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
francisco-del-rosario-sanchez: Sánchez was born in Santo Domingo on 9 March 1817. His mother, Olaya del Rosario Belén, was a free woman of colour; his father, Narciso Sánchez Ramona, a descendant of slaves, worked in the cattle and meat trade. The parents married only in 1819, which is why he bore his mother's surname before his father's. He was taught first by his mother and then by the Peruvian priest Gaspar Hernández. Juan Pablo Duarte, a classmate, recruited him to La Trinitaria, founded in 1838.

When Duarte and others left the country on 2 August 1843 to escape Haitian persecution, Sánchez, who was ill, stayed behind in hiding and took over the leadership of the movement. On the night of 27 February 1844 his men took the Ozama Fortress, and at the Puerta del Conde, after Matías Ramón Mella fired his blunderbuss, he raised the flag. He presided over the Central Government Board, and assured freed people who had mutinied under Santiago Basora that slavery would not return.

Pedro Santana marched on Santo Domingo and on 12 July 1844 drove the Trinitarios from the board. On 22 August Duarte, Sánchez and Mella were declared traitors and deported for life. He lived as a teacher in Curaçao until an amnesty granted by President Manuel Jimenes in 1848. Back home, he sided with Buenaventura Báez against Santana, was exiled again to Curaçao, returned in August 1856 and became governor of the province of Santo Domingo, and in 1859 was banished a third time, to Saint Thomas.

In 1861 Sánchez formed the Dominican Revolutionary Board and obtained from the Haitian president Fabre Geffrard passage through Haitian territory and weapons for a force of 500 men. He entered through Hondo Valle on 1 June 1861. When Haiti withdrew its support under threat from a Spanish squadron at Port-au-Prince, the expedition turned back. On 20 June Sánchez was ambushed near Hondo Valle by Santiago de Óleo, a former ally, wounded in the leg and groin, and captured.

A war council at San Juan under General Domingo Lazala tried the prisoners; Sánchez, conducting his own defence, asked that he alone be condemned. He was shot at San Juan de la Maguana on 4 July 1861 with some twenty companions, some of whom were finished off with machetes and clubs. Spain withdrew from the country in 1865. Dominicans honour him with Duarte and Mella as a founder of the republic, and the Order of Merit of Duarte, Sánchez and Mella bears his name.
franklin-d-roosevelt: Franklin Delano Roosevelt was born on 30 January 1882 in Hyde Park, New York, to James Roosevelt I and his second wife, Sara Ann Delano, who were sixth cousins from wealthy families. Apart from a stint in public school in Germany at nine, he was educated by tutors until 14, when he entered Groton School, whose headmaster Endicott Peabody urged students into public service. He graduated from Harvard University and married Eleanor Roosevelt, a niece of Theodore Roosevelt, on 17 March 1905.

In the Democratic landslide of 1910 Roosevelt won a surprising victory for a strongly Republican seat in the New York State Senate. In August 1921, at Campobello Island, he fell ill with what was diagnosed as polio, which left him permanently paralyzed from the waist down. He taught himself to walk short distances with iron braces and in 1926 established a rehabilitation centre at Warm Springs, Georgia.

He was elected governor of New York in 1928 by less than one percent. After winning the Democratic nomination on the fourth ballot in 1932, he pledged a new deal for the American people and defeated President Herbert Hoover.

Roosevelt had declined in health since at least 1940. On 12 April 1945, at the Little White House in Warm Springs, he said he had a terrific headache, slumped forward while sitting for a portrait, and was pronounced dead of a massive intracerebral hemorrhage, aged 63. The expansion of government programmes under Roosevelt redefined the role of government in the United States and permanently increased the power of the president at the expense of Congress. Surviving programmes include the Securities and Exchange Commission, the National Labor Relations Act and Social Security.
fyodor-dostoevsky: Fyodor Dostoevsky was born in Moscow on 11 November (Old Style 30 October) 1821, the second child of Dr Mikhail Dostoevsky and Maria Nechayeva. He grew up in the grounds of the Mariinsky Hospital for the Poor, where his father worked, and met patients from the lower end of Russian society when playing in the hospital gardens. His nanny read him sagas, fairy tales and legends, and his mother taught him to read from the Bible. His parents also introduced him to Pushkin, Schiller, Goethe, Cervantes, Walter Scott and Homer.

Dostoevsky completed his first novel, Poor Folk, in May 1845. His friend Dmitry Grigorovich took the manuscript to the poet Nikolay Nekrasov, who showed it to the critic Vissarion Belinsky, and Belinsky called it Russia's first social novel. It appeared on 15 January 1846 and sold well. He soon wrote The Double. He also read the French socialists Fourier, Cabet, Proudhon and Saint-Simon, but his Russian Orthodox faith could not accord with Belinsky's atheism and scientific materialism, and he parted from Belinsky and his circle.

In 1849 he was arrested for belonging to the Petrashevsky Circle, which discussed banned books critical of Tsarist Russia. He was sentenced to death, but the sentence was commuted at the last moment. He spent four years in a Siberian hard labour camp, which inspired The House of the Dead, and then six years of compulsory military service in exile. Later he edited magazines of his own and wrote A Writer's Diary, travelled in Western Europe and developed a gambling addiction that brought financial hardship.

His major novels include Crime and Punishment (1866), The Idiot (1869), Demons (1872), The Adolescent (1875) and The Brothers Karamazov (1880). Notes from Underground, a novella of 1864, is considered one of the first works of existentialist literature. After his release from prison he put religious themes, especially those of Russian Orthodoxy, into his writing. His fiction takes up suicide, poverty, human manipulation and morality, and depicts the chaotic sociopolitical order of contemporary Russia.

Mikhail Bakhtin saw polyphony, the simultaneous presence of several narrative voices and perspectives, as an important element of his style and a major advance in the novel. Friedrich Nietzsche called him the only psychologist from whom he had something to learn, and Sigmund Freud ranked him second only to William Shakespeare among creative writers. He died on 9 February (Old Style 28 January) 1881 after a series of pulmonary hemorrhages, and asked that the parable of the Prodigal Son be read to his children.
